title: Broken Promises and Nehemiah's Last Reforms
summary: After the reading of the law excluding Ammonites and Moabites from the assembly, the chapter turns to Nehemiah's second term. Returning from the Persian court, he finds that the priest Eliashib has given Tobiah a room in the temple, that the Levites have gone unpaid and left for their fields, that Jerusalem trades on the Sabbath, and that Jews have married women from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab, even within the high priest's family. He throws out Tobiah's goods, restores the tithes, shuts the gates on the Sabbath, confronts the men who married foreign women, and ends the book asking God to remember him with favor.
story: The book could have ended with the joy of chapter 12. Instead it closes with an honest look at how quickly a community can drift. Nearly every problem Nehemiah addresses here is a pledge the people made in chapter 10: they had promised not to intermarry with the surrounding peoples (10:30), not to buy on the Sabbath (10:31), and not to neglect the house of God (10:39). Now all three promises have been broken. The walls stand, but the people inside them have not been made new. The Old Testament's historical narrative effectively ends here, with the people back in the land, the temple standing, and the heart of the community still in need of the deeper renewal the prophets had promised.
historical:
Verse 6 gives the chronology: Nehemiah went back to Artaxerxes in the king's thirty-second year, about 433 BC, after twelve years as governor (5:14). He returned to Jerusalem some time later, how long is not stated. The Persian king is called king of Babylon because Babylon was one of his capitals and the title was among those the Persian kings held after Cyrus conquered the city.

The people involved are familiar. Eliashib is probably the high priest of 3:1 and 12:10, though some think the Eliashib of verse 4 was a different priest in charge of the storerooms. Tobiah, the Ammonite opponent of chapters 2 to 6, had ties by marriage with Jerusalem's leading families (6:17-18). Sanballat, governor of Samaria, is called the Horonite, probably after Beth-horon, a town northwest of Jerusalem. A grandson of the high priest marrying Sanballat's daughter (verse 28) tied the priestly family to the political leader of the rival province. Many scholars note that the prophet Malachi addresses the same problems, including neglected tithes, careless priests, and marriages outside the covenant (Malachi 2:10-16; 3:8-10), and suggest he prophesied around this time, though his exact date is uncertain.
cultural:
The law read in verses 1-2 is Deuteronomy 23:3-5, which barred Ammonites and Moabites from the assembly of the Lord because they had not helped Israel on the road from Egypt and had hired Balaam to curse them (Numbers 22 to 24). The temple storerooms were chambers around the courts used to store offerings and supplies; giving one to Tobiah, an Ammonite and an enemy of the rebuilding, turned holy space into a private office for an outsider. Without the tithes, the Levites and singers had no income, since the law gave them no farmland of their own, so they went back to whatever fields they had and the temple service lapsed.

Sabbath rest was one of the clearest marks of Israel's identity. In the busy market town Jerusalem was becoming, the pressure to trade was strong, especially with foreign merchants, like the men of Tyre, a Phoenician trading city, who did not keep the Sabbath themselves. Nehemiah's solution was practical: close the gates at dusk on Friday, when the Sabbath began. The complaint about children who could not speak the language of Judah (verse 24) shows why intermarriage was more than a private matter: in a small community under foreign rule, losing the language meant losing access to the Scriptures and to the community's worship and identity.
literary: The chapter consists of an introductory scene (verses 1-3) followed by four reform episodes, each introduced by a time phrase (“Before this”, “In those days”) and each dealing with a problem, Nehemiah's response, and, in three of the four, a short prayer: the temple storerooms and tithes (4-14), the Sabbath (15-22), and mixed marriages (23-29), with a summary of reforms (30-31). The prayers asking God to remember (verses 14, 22, 29, 31) give the chapter its rhythm, and the book ends with the last of them: “Remember me, O my God, with favor.” It is a deliberately unresolved ending. There is no celebration, only a tired leader still working and asking God to take note.

outline.t: The law excluding Ammonites and Moabites is read
Tobiah's room in the temple is cleared
Marriages with foreign women and the priest's son-in-law
Summary of reforms and a final prayer

doctrines.note: The chapter shows how quickly sincere promises can be broken. The people's failures follow the same patterns their forefathers fell into, as Nehemiah points out (verses 18 and 26). Reform of outward structures does not by itself change the heart.

The Sabbath, the tithes, and the marriage laws are treated as essential to the community's faithfulness. Nehemiah's appeal to Solomon (verse 26) shows that even the greatest of Israel's kings was drawn into sin by ignoring God's commands.

Nehemiah says the priests “have defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites” (verse 29). The priesthood was itself a covenant trust (Numbers 25:12-13; Malachi 2:4-8), and those who held it were accountable for guarding it.

words.note: Shabbat, Sabbath, the seventh day of rest. It appears ten times in this chapter. The Sabbath marked Israel as God's people, recalling both creation (Exodus 20:11) and deliverance from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). Nehemiah treats Sabbath-breaking as a repetition of the sins that led to the exile (verse 18).

Chalal, to profane. The verb means to treat something holy as common. Nehemiah charges the nobles with profaning the Sabbath (verses 17-18). The concern is not only rule-breaking but treating what God set apart as if it were ordinary.

Nokhri, foreign. The word describes women from other nations whom Jewish men had married (verses 26-27). In context the problem is religious rather than ethnic: Nehemiah's example is Solomon, whose foreign wives turned his heart to other gods (1 Kings 11:1-8).

Riv, to contend or rebuke. Nehemiah contends with the officials (verse 11), the nobles (verse 17), and the men who married foreign women (verse 25). The word is used for legal disputes, and it presents Nehemiah as bringing a formal charge on God's behalf.

christ: The ending of Nehemiah shows the limits of reform. A good leader could clear the temple, restore the tithes, shut the gates, and rebuke the priests, but he could not change the people's hearts, and he ends the book asking God to remember him. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one who does what Nehemiah could not. He too cleared the temple of those who used it for trade (John 2:13-17), but he also promised a new heart through his Spirit. He is the high priest who does not defile his office (Hebrews 7:26), the Lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28), and the one who brings Gentiles into the people of God, not by ignoring God's holiness but by making them holy (Ephesians 2:11-22). The contrast is the New Testament's own reading of the story rather than a prediction in Nehemiah.

hard.q: Was Nehemiah right to beat people and pull out their hair, and how does his opposition to foreign marriages fit with Ruth the Moabite?
hard.a:
Verse 25 describes Nehemiah cursing, beating, and pulling the hair of men who had married foreign women. The text reports this without comment, and readers should not assume that everything a biblical character does is approved. Some interpreters see Nehemiah's actions as the harsh but lawful discipline of a governor confronting a threat to the community's survival, in a culture where public shaming was a normal punishment. Others see here a zealous leader whose methods went beyond what was right, and note that the book ends with Nehemiah asking for mercy rather than claiming vindication.

The question about foreign marriages is also real, since Ruth, a Moabite woman, married Boaz and became the great-grandmother of David. The difference lies in faith. Ruth committed herself to Israel's God (Ruth 1:16), and the concern in Deuteronomy 7 and in Nehemiah is marriage to people who continued to worship other gods, which had drawn Solomon into idolatry. The issue was religious faithfulness rather than ethnicity. Nehemiah's chapter still raises hard questions about how the exclusion of Ammonites and Moabites was applied, and interpreters differ on how strictly it was meant to operate; later Scripture, especially Isaiah 56:3-7, promises that foreigners who hold fast to God's covenant will be welcomed in his house.

questions: The people broke the promises of chapter 10 within a few years. Which of your own commitments to God are most at risk of quietly slipping?
Nehemiah repeatedly asked God to remember him. What does it mean to entrust your work and your reputation to God rather than seeking recognition from others?
Nehemiah worried that children who could not speak the language of Judah would lose their faith. What practices pass faith on to the next generation in your home or community?
